title: Approximate statistical tests for comparing supervised classification learning algorithms
harvard_reference: Dietterich, T.G. (1998) 'Approximate statistical tests for comparing supervised classification learning algorithms', Neural Computation, 10(7), pp. 1895-1923. doi:10.1162/089976698300017197.
abstract_summary: The paper reviews five approximate statistical tests for deciding whether one learning algorithm outperforms another on a given task and compares them experimentally on their Type I error (falsely detecting a difference when none exists) and their power. Two widely used tests, a difference-of-two-proportions test and a paired-differences t test over several random train/test splits (the 'resampled t test'), are found to have high Type I error in some situations and the author says they should never be used. A paired t test over 10-fold cross-validation has somewhat elevated Type I error. McNemar's test has low Type I error, and a newly proposed 5x2cv paired t test (five repetitions of two-fold cross-validation) also has acceptable Type I error. On power, the cross-validated t test is the strongest, and 5x2cv is slightly more powerful than McNemar's test. The recommended test depends on computational cost: when an algorithm can be run only once, McNemar's test is the only one with acceptable Type I error; when it can be run ten times, 5x2cv is recommended because it is slightly more powerful and directly measures variation due to the choice of training set.

claims_supported.claim: McNemar's test on paired predictions from a single test set has acceptable Type I error for comparing two classifiers, whereas the resampled t-test has elevated Type I error.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (verbatim text obtained from PubMed PMID 9744903 and reproduced identically by OpenAlex). The abstract states that the paired-differences t test based on taking several random train/test splits (which the paper's tables label 'Resampled t') has a high probability of Type I error in certain situations and should never be used, that McNemar's test 'is shown to have low type I error', and that for algorithms that can be executed only once (i.e. a single training run evaluated on a single test set) McNemar's test is the only test with acceptable Type I error. The claim's wording 'elevated' is if anything milder than the paper's own conclusion ('high probability of type I error ... should never be used'). The single-test-set framing matches the paper's 'executed only once' recommendation; McNemar's test in the paper is computed from the two classifiers' paired correct/incorrect outcomes on the same held-out test set.

verification_notes: Metadata verified via CrossRef (DOI 10.1162/089976698300017197; MIT Press; ISSN 0899-7667 / 1530-888X), Semantic Scholar (DBLP journals/neco/Dietterich98; PMID 9744903), OpenAlex (volume 10, issue 7, pp. 1895-1923; ~3,800 citations) and PubMed E-utilities (Neural Comput. 1998 Sep 15;10(7):1895-1923). Semantic Scholar returned a null abstract (publisher restriction), so the verbatim abstract was taken from PubMed and cross-checked word for word against OpenAlex's inverted index. The MIT Press landing page and article PDF return HTTP 403 to automated fetches. An open copy of the PDF (sci2s.ugr.es) was downloaded but its fonts use non-Unicode encodings, so body text could not be extracted; only figure/table labels came through, which do confirm the five tests are named 'McNemar', 'Prop Test', 'Resampled t', 'Xval t' and '5x2cv t' in the paper. Claim assessment therefore rests on the verbatim abstract, which states the relevant findings explicitly. Author affiliation on the PubMed record: Oregon State University, Department of Computer Science. Lead reference was accurate apart from missing page numbers and DOI, now added.
caveats: The paper's Type I error results are empirical (simulation-style experiments on a limited set of tasks and learning algorithms in 1998), not analytical guarantees; the author frames all five tests as approximate. The paper also finds McNemar's test is slightly less powerful than the 5x2cv test and, for algorithms that can be run ten times, recommends 5x2cv rather than McNemar. When citing this for a single-holdout-split model comparison (e.g. one Telco Customer Churn test set), it is accurate to say McNemar's test is the appropriate choice among those studied, but the report should not imply McNemar's test is the most powerful option overall. The paper concerns classification error rates on a fixed test set; it says nothing about churn prediction specifically.
